newsitem.title: USA: Clinton readies for Mideast summit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton readies for Mideast summit.

text.p: President Bill Clinton readied on Monday to host a politically risky two-day Mideast summit in bid to end a new round of violence between Israelis and Palestinians and salvage a fragile peace process.
Clinton late on Monday was to meet in the private residence of the White House with Jordan's King Hussein to discuss the two-day emergency summit that begins on Tuesday.

Fearful the latest crisis will undermine peace efforts in the region, Clinton announced the summit to bring Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat to the White House for face-to-face talks.

Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak -- a key voice for moderate Arabs -- declined to attend the hastily called gathering but dispatched Foreign Minister Amr Moussa to Washington, although he will have no direct role in the talks.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the discussions would focus on several key questions, "How can we restore calm? What can we do to bring an end to the violence? How can we re-engage the (peace) process?"

Arafat and Mubarak, who met in Egypt on Monday before Arafat travelled on to Europe and Washington, had wanted to postpone the summit pending assurances it would bring firm guarantees of Israeli gestures toward the Palestinians.

But McCurry told reporters, "We attached no preconditions to the discussions but we asked only that the leaders arrive only in a frame of mind to address the fundamental questions that will be before them."
"We are not excluding items from consideration for this conference," he said. "We fully expect all sides to bring the issues up that are relevant."

The summit takes place not only against a backdrop of a sudden resumption of Israeli-Palestinian violence but in the midst of the U.S. election campaign, with Clinton under challenge by Republican Bob Dole in the Nov. 5 balloting.
Fighting erupted in the West Bank and Gaza last week after Israel opened a pedestrian tunnel to archaeological sites by Jerusalem's Temple Mount, sacred to both Judaism and Islam.
Fifty-five Palestinians and 14 Israelis were killed in five days of clashes.

"It's clear to me that the Middle East peace process is in a state of crisis," Secretary of State Warren Christopher said. "The President took an extraordinary step in inviting the parties to come here to Washington for these meetings."
But Christopher sought to play down chances for a major breakthrough at the Washington talks.
"I think we ought to recognise the limitations," he said before talks with Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus. "The parties are quite estranged and raw because of the violence and killings."

He described the basic aims of the summit as "first that the parties will begin to talk together again, second that they will commit to end the violence, and third that they will find the basis for resuming negotiations."
Despite the pressures of his re-election campaign schedule, including a televised debate with Dole next Sunday night, Clinton cleared his calendar through the middle of the week to act as mediator.

Dole issued a statement saying that "American strategy for this meeting ... must be clear and decisive. We must demand an unconditional end to the violence. Our friend Israel must not be asked to make concessions as a means of restoring order."
Although the Republican challenger's statement was clearly in support of Israel, most public opinion polls show Jewish-American voters favour Clinton in the election.

One of the highlights of Clinton's presidency was his shepherding of Arafat and the late Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin into an "historic handshake" at 1993 White House ceremonies in which Israel and the Palestinians signed a peace accord designed to end a long and bloody feud.
Clinton, however, favoured former Prime Minister Shimon Peres in Israel's May elections -- leaving him with limited influence in his dealings with Netanyahu.
